title: U.S. House · Texas's 13th District

context.text: Incumbent Republican Ronny Jackson defeated Chasity Wedgeworth in the Republican primary. Mark Nair, a former Amarillo City Councilman, won the Democratic primary unopposed.

candidates.name: Ronny L. Jackson
candidates.ballotNote: Won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary over Chasity Wedgeworth

summary.text: Ronny Jackson is the Republican incumbent seeking re-election in Texas's 13th District. A physician raised in Levelland, he served as a Navy medical officer and worked in the White House Medical Unit, serving as physician to the president under Barack Obama and Donald Trump before being elected to Congress in 2020. He serves on the House Intelligence, Armed Services, Agriculture and Foreign Affairs committees.

background.text: According to his House biography, Jackson was raised in Levelland, Texas, and worked as a roustabout in the West Texas oilfields while paying his way through undergraduate school.
He earned a bachelor's degree in marine biology from Texas A&M University in 1991 and a medical degree from the University of Texas Medical Branch in 1995.

After medical school he began active-duty service in the U.S. Navy, trained in undersea medicine, and served at postings from Panama City, Florida, to Sigonella, Italy; he later completed an emergency medicine residency and deployed to Iraq to lead resuscitative medicine for a Combat Surgical Shock Trauma Platoon. Ballotpedia lists his service as the U.S. Navy Reserve and the U.S. Marine Corps.

He served in the White House Medical Unit during George W. Bush's administration, later became its director, and served as Physician to the President under Barack Obama (concluding his duties as director in December 2014) and Donald Trump.

In January 2019 President Trump appointed him Chief Medical Advisor and Assistant to the President. His House biography says he retired from the Navy as a Rear Admiral in December 2019 after 25 years of service.

The Denton Record-Chronicle reported that Jackson was reportedly demoted from Navy rear admiral to captain in 2022 after allegations of inappropriate behavior during his time as a White House physician, and that his rank was restored in 2025; the article does not include a response from Jackson.

He was elected to represent Texas's 13th District in November 2020, succeeding Mac Thornberry, and took office in 2021. His committee assignments are Intelligence (Permanent Select), Agriculture, Armed Services and Foreign Affairs.
In the March 3, 2026 Republican primary, Jackson defeated Chasity Wedgeworth with about 89% of the vote.
According to his House biography, he has been married to his wife Jane for over 30 years and they have three children.

record.text: Serves on the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, chairing its Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations and also sitting on its Central Intelligence Agency Subcommittee, for the 119th Congress (2025-2026).
Serves on the House Committee on Armed Services, chairing its Subcommittee on Intelligence and Special Operations, and on its Subcommittee on Seapower and Projection Forces, for the 119th Congress.
Serves on the Committee on Agriculture, including its Subcommittees on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology and on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry, for the 119th Congress.

candidates.name: Mark Nair
candidates.ballotNote: Won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary unopposed

summary.text: Mark Nair is the Democratic nominee challenging incumbent Ronny Jackson in Texas's 13th District. Describing himself as a former Amarillo city councilman, inventor, entrepreneur and educator, he worked for 23 years in entertainment distribution and later taught economics and software development at Amarillo College. His campaign focuses on healthcare, government accountability, and education.

background.text: Nair earned a high school diploma from Westfield High School, a bachelor's degree from Texas A&M University in 1988 and a graduate degree from Texas A&M in 1991.
In his Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey, he says he worked for 23 years in the entertainment distribution business at a company called Anderson Merchandisers.
He says he has taught Economics and Software Development at the college level and won the Faculty Excellence Award at Amarillo College in 2020.

He describes himself as an inventor with a few technological patents and a member of the National Academy of Inventors, and says he helps mentor startup companies at the Texas Tech Innovation Hub and the National Science Foundation.
Nair is a former member of the Amarillo City Council.
He has lived in Amarillo for more than 30 years with his wife Suzanne; he says they have three children, all born in Amarillo.
Nair ran unopposed in the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary and received 28,198 votes.

priorities.text: Separate healthcare from employment through a national health care plan, saying the current system makes healthcare about insurance rather than health.
Government accountability: remove corporate and dark money from politics, ban congressional stock trading, and impose term limits on elected officials.
Education and economic opportunity, including opposition to dismantling the Department of Education and support for a national jobs program.

positions.summary: His platform says he will work toward Medicare for All.
positions.quote: He'll work toward Medicare for All, making healthcare costs fair, reasonable, and affordable for every American.

positions.summary: His platform says tariffs belong with Congress rather than the president and describes current tariffs as having raised farmers' costs and cost them export markets.
positions.quote: Tariffs belong in Congress's hands, not the president's.

positions.summary: His platform criticizes federal spending on detention, calls for an end to for-profit detention, and calls for a path to citizenship for law-abiding families.
positions.quote: While our roads crumble, our water systems age, and our rural hospitals close, our government is pouring billions into detention camps. That is a choice. And it is the wrong one.
